claim_a: The company filed that it 'commenced offering products for sale on its Web site in July 1995' and that 'for the period from inception through July 1995, the Company had no sales', i.e. recognised trading began in July 1995
claim_a_source: S0801 Amazon.com Form S-1 (original), acc. 0000891618-97-001309, filed 1997-03-24; same wording in S0802 and S0803
claim_b: Amazon's own launch release reported that 'in just its first four weeks of operation, the company shipped books to customers in all 50 states and more than 45 countries', which counts back to about early September 1995; and, third, the folkloric day-level launch of 16 July 1995
claim_b_source: S1701 press release dated 1995-10-04 (indexed 1995-10-03); the 16-July leg rests on S0004 HistoryLink (2025) restating S0605 Seattle Times (2005) and S0206 Stone (2013)
why_they_differ: Three readings, none excluded: (i) public launch versus commencement of sales, July being a restricted or soft-opened trading month; (ii) loose PR arithmetic off an unstated base, since a 16 July opening would turn four weeks into eleven; (iii) both legs are company self-reports, so the tension is between two statements by one author, not between a claim and a measurement. The filing phrase 'through July 1995' is itself ambiguous and can place ZERO recognised sales in July. The 16-July day has no primary support at all (COR-09)
evidence_weight: Leg A is Tier 1, audited, present in three accessions of one registration statement (S0801/S0802/S0803 - same lineage as S0801, so a restatement and not a second confirmation per method §3's filing-lineage rule; AUDIT 5 A-B1), and it controls revenue dating. Leg B1 is Tier 1 and contemporaneous and is the only dated 1995 statement about when outside demand appeared. Leg B2 is Tier 2/3, ten-plus years downstream and derivative of a single lineage. S0002 (Kaphan 2011) adds a non-documentary third leg, a soft launch a couple of months before July
best_supported_interpretation: Report two distinct facts and compute no launch date: recognised trading from July 1995 (High), and the company's own claim of 50-state and 45-country shipping within four weeks as of 4 October 1995 (High that it was claimed, Low that it was verified). Carried as ONE conflict with three legs, not as three conflicts (COR-11.5)
residual_uncertainty: Which event 'operation' counts from; whether any July orders were recognised in a later period; whether the release understated its own age for effect; whether an invite-only order in April 1995 predates every official dating
confidence: Medium on the reconciliation; High that the conflict is unresolved

claim_a: The first non-employee order was placed on 3 April 1995 by John Wainwright for Douglas Hofstadter's Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies at $27.95, after Shel Kaphan e-mailed him to create an account and order books
claim_a_source: S0611 MarketWatch (2015) and S0610 The Atlantic (2012), one interview cycle relayed again by S0613 Yahoo Creators (2025)
claim_b: Every company statement places the first sale in July 1995 at the earliest; the popular canon fixes the day as 16 July 1995; the object mutates to a science textbook; the 2007 company timeline says only '1995 July / Amazon.com Sells First Book'; and a circulated prospectus sentence, 'we officially launched our Web site in July 1995 and shipped our first book in August 1995', is absent from all five SEC documents
claim_b_source: S0801 (no sales through July 1995); S1701 and S1703 (company dating); S0004 and S0605 (16 July, science textbook); S1710 (2007 IR timeline)
why_they_differ: Anniversary compression; conflation of first ORDER with first SHIPMENT; a curated company PR event dressed as an observation; and at least one quotation with no document behind it. S0203 separately reports a six-week beta of about 300 charged friend-and-family orders before opening, which contradicts the very idea of a single first sale, and the object mutates across tellings (Hofstadter's AI essays versus a science textbook, Mr versus John Wainwright)
evidence_weight: None of the variants is contemporaneous. The buyer account is Tier 2, internally self-contradicting because S0610 prints both 3 April 1995 and Amazon's own July 1995 dating, and its three articles descend from ONE interview. The 2007 timeline is company-authored but from 2007. The August-1995 sentence is unverifiable. Only the $27.95 price is common to all tellings
best_supported_interpretation: Hofstadter's book is the best-attested first NON-EMPLOYEE order and 'science textbook' is a degraded variant of the same story; 'shipped our first book in August 1995' is untraced and unusable. Because real first transactions were probably insider beta purchases, NO individual may be certified as the first customer
residual_uncertainty: No Amazon document naming a first title or a first customer has been found, and the company never identified one during Stage 1. Whether the April 1995 order sat inside a closed beta is unknown
confidence: Medium on the Wainwright order as an event; Low on every day-level and title-level canon

claim_a: Bezos read that Web usage was growing 2,300 percent a year and that fact triggered the founding; the earliest retrievable printed version is the Los Angeles Times of 1997-07-20
claim_a_source: S0202 Los Angeles Times (Littman), restated by S0203 Sheff (conducted 1999, published 2000) and S0210
claim_b: The number is a misreading of cumulative factors: John Quarterman's Matrix News of February 1994 reported bytes up by a factor of 2,057 and packets up by 2,560 between January 1993 and January 1994, and Bezos interpolated a factor of roughly 2,300, i.e. a 230,000 percent increase, so the signature figure is a math error
claim_b_source: S0206 Brad Stone (2013), resting on S0201 Matrix News, which has never been examined at source
why_they_differ: The founder refrain restates a cumulative twelve-month multiple as an annual percentage growth rate and compresses a multi-week research process into a found fact. Later repetitions are not independent sources: three printed tellings descend from the founder's own account and the only documentary derivation descends from a book
evidence_weight: Stone's version is the only one naming a document, a date and a calculation, and even it is unexamined at source. Against both, three contemporaneous measurements do not support 2,300 percent a year: Netcraft's 603,367 responding sites in December 1996 and 1,117,259 in June 1997 (S0406, S0407), i.e. about 85 percent in six months; IDC's roughly 35 million users at end-1996 inside S0801; and the CERN-era server list in the tens (S0401). The figure is verified ABSENT from the on-disk original S-1 (COR-11.7)
best_supported_interpretation: Record the 2,300 percent as a FOUNDER CLAIM OF UNSTATED AND UNTRACEABLE PROVENANCE; the defensible statement is that a 1993-94 Web traffic series exhibiting roughly 2,000-fold annual growth convinced him the medium was inflecting. It may never enter the metrics table as history
residual_uncertainty: Whether Matrix News itself ever printed '2,300%' is UNKNOWN because the newsletter has not been examined, and no 1994-dated document ties the number to the decision at all
confidence: High on the challenge to the figure; Medium on Stone's reconstruction; High that no traceable origin exists

claim_a: A titled, page-counted 91-page 'roadmap' named 'Future of Computer Stores' was written in 1994 and set out the everything-store plan
claim_a_source: no source: exact-phrase searches return only the aggregation layer registered as S1802, with zero authoritative hits, no repository, no sale record and no quoted line
claim_b: The evidence ladder tops out at rung 3, founder description only: a laptop document in 1997, a prose first draft written in the car in 1999, and an Excel projection in 2013, three mutually inconsistent physical accounts of one artifact by one witness. why_they_differ: The titled artifact has no lineage whatsoever, and its likeliest mechanism is a genuine but unremarkable circulated startup plan, progressively inflated in the retelling into a named, page-counted prophetic document once the outcome made such an artifact valuable. evidence_weight: Tier 5 for the roadmap as an artifact, against Tier 1 for the hard negative control: the audited S-1 contains neither the word 'roadmap' nor the phrase 'business plan' in 1.44 MB, states its founding purpose as online BOOK retailing, and relegates category expansion to a Risk Factor. Repeated copying is one source, and Stone's Chapter 1 neither describes a 91-page plan nor quotes any planning document

Section C may state ONLY that Bezos described drafting a plan during the drive and that no copy, text, page count or title has ever surfaced; it may NOT name a roadmap, a 91-page notebook or 'Future of Computer Stores', and may not attribute an everything-store conception to 1994 except as a D. E. Shaw conversation recalled in 2013, Bezos's own statement on scope being 'at first, all we knew is that we were going to sell books'
